```{r new_task_type-001, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
lgr::get_logger("mlr3")$set_threshold("warn")
```

The [Custom Learning Problems](custom_task_type.html) article shows how to use the generic `TaskTorch` for learning problems beyond classification and regression.
This is quick, but the `"torch"` task type cannot tell different learning problems apart, so {mlr3} cannot check that learners, tasks, and measures fit together.
The alternative is to register a proper new task type with {mlr3}, as is done, e.g., by {mlr3proba} for survival analysis.
This article shows the steps that are needed so that the learners of {mlr3torch} can be used for such a task type.
As a running example, we use a very simple task type `"count"` for count data, i.e., Poisson regression.
Note that the implementation in this article is only a minimal one that is meant to illustrate the required steps, and it skips some of the checks and functionality that a proper implementation should have.
A task type that is used in practice requires more care, e.g., input checks (such as that the target is a non-negative integer), support for additional predict types and measures, as well as tests.

```{r new_task_type-002}
library(mlr3torch)
library(data.table)
library(R6)
```

## Registering the Task Type with mlr3

A task type in {mlr3} consists of a `Task`, a `Prediction` and a `Measure` class, which have to be registered in `mlr_reflections`.
These are independent of {mlr3torch}, so we only keep them as short as possible here.
For our count task, the target is a single integer column.

```{r new_task_type-003}
TaskCount = R6Class("TaskCount", inherit = TaskSupervised,
  public = list(
    initialize = function(id, backend, target, label = NA_character_) {
      super$initialize(id = id, task_type = "count", backend = backend, target = target,
        label = label)
    },
    truth = function(rows = NULL) super$truth(rows)[[1L]]
  )
)
```

A prediction for this task type contains the predicted rate as the `response`.
The data of a prediction is stored in an object of class `PredictionData<Type>`, for which a few S3 generics of {mlr3} have to be implemented.

```{r new_task_type-004}
PredictionCount = R6Class("PredictionCount", inherit = Prediction,
  public = list(
    initialize = function(task = NULL, row_ids = task$row_ids, truth = task$truth(),
      response = NULL, check = TRUE) {
      pdata = structure(list(row_ids = row_ids, truth = truth, response = response),
        class = c("PredictionDataCount", "PredictionData"))
      if (check) pdata = check_prediction_data(pdata)
      self$task_type = "count"
      self$data = pdata
      self$predict_types = "response"
    }
  ),
  active = list(
    response = function() {
      if (is.null(self$data$response)) rep(NA_real_, length(self$data$row_ids)) else self$data$response
    }
  )
)

as.data.table.PredictionCount = function(x, ...) {
  data.table(row_ids = x$row_ids, truth = x$truth, response = x$response)
}

check_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, ...) {
  pdata$row_ids = checkmate::assert_integerish(pdata$row_ids, coerce = TRUE)
  pdata$response = checkmate::assert_numeric(unname(pdata$response), lower = 0,
    len = length(pdata$row_ids), null.ok = TRUE)
  pdata
}

is_missing_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, ...) {
  pdata$row_ids[is.na(pdata$response)]
}

filter_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, row_ids, ...) {
  keep = pdata$row_ids %in% row_ids
  pdata[c("row_ids", "truth", "response")] = lapply(pdata[c("row_ids", "truth", "response")],
    function(x) x[keep])
  pdata
}

c.PredictionDataCount = function(..., keep_duplicates = TRUE) {
  dots = list(...)
  pdata = lapply(c(row_ids = "row_ids", truth = "truth", response = "response"),
    function(nm) unlist(lapply(dots, `[[`, nm)))
  if (!keep_duplicates) {
    keep = !duplicated(pdata$row_ids, fromLast = TRUE)
    pdata = lapply(pdata, function(x) x[keep])
  }
  structure(pdata, class = c("PredictionDataCount", "PredictionData"))
}

as_prediction.PredictionDataCount = function(x, check = FALSE, ...) {
  PredictionCount$new(row_ids = x$row_ids, truth = x$truth, response = x$response, check = check)
}
```

In a package, these methods would be registered via `S3method()` in the `NAMESPACE` file.
In this article, we register them manually.

```{r new_task_type-005}
for (generic in c("check_prediction_data", "is_missing_prediction_data",
  "filter_prediction_data", "c", "as_prediction")) {
  registerS3method(generic, "PredictionDataCount", get(paste0(generic, ".PredictionDataCount")))
}
registerS3method("as.data.table", "PredictionCount", as.data.table.PredictionCount)
```

As the default measure, we use the Poisson deviance.

```{r new_task_type-006}
MeasureCountDeviance = R6Class("MeasureCountDeviance", inherit = Measure,
  public = list(
    initialize = function() {
      super$initialize(id = "count.deviance", task_type = "count",
        predict_type = "response", range = c(0, Inf), minimize = TRUE)
    }
  ),
  private = list(
    .score = function(prediction, ...) {
      y = prediction$truth
      mu = prediction$response
      2 * mean(ifelse(y == 0, 0, y * log(y / mu)) - (y - mu))
    }
  )
)
mlr_measures$add("count.deviance", MeasureCountDeviance)
```

Finally, we register the task type in `mlr_reflections`.
For simplicity, we copy most of the settings from the regression task type.

```{r new_task_type-007}
mlr_reflections$task_types = setkeyv(rbind(mlr_reflections$task_types, data.table(
  type = "count", package = "countpkg", task = "TaskCount", learner = "Learner",
  prediction = "PredictionCount", prediction_data = "PredictionDataCount",
  measure = "MeasureCountDeviance"
), fill = TRUE), "type")
for (registry in c("task_col_roles", "task_properties", "learner_properties",
  "measure_properties")) {
  mlr_reflections[[registry]]$count = mlr_reflections[[registry]]$regr
}
mlr_reflections$learner_predict_types$count = list(response = "response")
mlr_reflections$default_measures$count = "count.deviance"
```

## Supporting the Task Type in mlr3torch

{mlr3torch} has no separate learner classes per task type: all learners inherit from `LearnerTorch`, which takes the `task_type` as a construction argument.
The task-type-specific behavior is defined by three S3 generics, which dispatch on the class of the task:

* `output_dim_for()`: How many output units the network needs.
* `get_target_batchgetter()`: How the target is converted to a tensor.
* `encode_prediction()`: How the output of the network is converted into the data of a prediction.

For Poisson regression, the network has a single output unit, which we interpret as the log-rate.

```{r new_task_type-008}
output_dim_for.TaskCount = function(x, ...) 1L

get_target_batchgetter.TaskCount = function(task, ...) {
  function(data) torch_tensor(data[[1L]], dtype = torch_float32())$unsqueeze(2)
}

encode_prediction.TaskCount = function(task, network_output, predict_type, ...) {
  list(response = as.numeric(torch_exp(network_output)$cpu()))
}

registerS3method("output_dim_for", "TaskCount", output_dim_for.TaskCount)
registerS3method("get_target_batchgetter", "TaskCount", get_target_batchgetter.TaskCount)
registerS3method("encode_prediction", "TaskCount", encode_prediction.TaskCount)
```

Next, we need a loss for the new task type.
We add the Poisson negative log-likelihood to the `mlr3torch_losses` dictionary and declare that it can be used for the `"count"` task type.

```{r new_task_type-009}
mlr3torch_losses$add("poisson", function() {
  TorchLoss$new(torch_loss = nn_poisson_nll_loss, task_types = "count", id = "poisson",
    label = "Poisson NLL", man = "torch::nn_poisson_nll_loss")
})
```

Without further information, a learner for the new task type requires the loss to be passed explicitly:

```{r new_task_type-010, error = TRUE}
LearnerTorchMLP$new(task_type = "count")
```

To make it the default loss for the task type, we register its id in `mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses`, which also holds the defaults for classification and regression.

```{r new_task_type-011}
mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses$count = "poisson"
mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses
```

Finally, we add the learners we want to offer for the new task type to the `mlr_learners` dictionary, here the multi-layer perceptron:

```{r new_task_type-012}
mlr_learners$add("count.mlp", function(...) LearnerTorchMLP$new(task_type = "count", ...))
```

## Using the New Task Type

We simulate some count data, where the rate depends on two features.

```{r new_task_type-013}
set.seed(42)
n = 1000
dat = data.table(x1 = runif(n, -1, 1), x2 = runif(n, -1, 1))
dat$y = rpois(n, exp(0.5 + dat$x1 - 0.5 * dat$x2))
task = TaskCount$new("sim_count", backend = dat, target = "y")
task
```

The learner can now be constructed without specifying the loss, and the measure defaults to the Poisson deviance.

```{r new_task_type-014}
learner = lrn("count.mlp", epochs = 50, batch_size = 32, neurons = 16, opt.lr = 0.01)
learner$loss
```

Because the task type is registered with {mlr3}, the learner can be resampled, tuned, and benchmarked like any other learner, and a mismatch between task types is caught.

```{r new_task_type-015}
rr = resample(task, learner, rsmp("holdout"))
rr$aggregate()
head(as.data.table(rr$prediction()))
```

```{r new_task_type-016, error = TRUE}
learner$train(tsk("mtcars"))
```
